# Bowel cancer screening: what the test can and can't tell you

*Test fixture written for this repo. The numbers are illustrative.*

Bowel cancer screening uses a simple home test that looks for tiny amounts of blood in a stool sample. It is offered every two years to people aged 50 to 74.

Out of 1,000 people aged 50 to 74, about 30 will develop bowel cancer over the next 25 years if none of them is screened. Regular screening finds many cancers early, when they are easier to treat. Over 25 years, screening every two years finds roughly 60% of the cancers that would develop, early enough to treat more easily.

The test is not perfect. Blood can come from other causes, such as polyps that would never become cancer, or haemorrhoids. Each time someone does the test, about 5 in 100 get a positive result. Most positive results are not cancer. Over many rounds of screening, about a third of people who keep screening will get at least one positive result. That leads to a colonoscopy, which is usually safe but uncomfortable, and carries a small risk.

People often think a positive result means they probably have cancer. In fact, fewer than 1 in 20 positive results turn out to be cancer.

Doing the test regularly matters more than doing it once. Missing rounds lets cancers grow without being found. Talk to your doctor if you have symptoms, whatever your last test said.
